papers.title_zh: 使用混合卷积神经网络的皮肤疾病分类
papers.source_body_en: This research aims to classify skin diseases using a hybrid Convolutional Neural Network (CNN) method. Hybrid CNN is an integration between the CNN model and machine learning methods. The classification methods used include logistic regression, random forest, and XGBoost. The highest performance results are obtained when using ResNet as a feature extraction and logistic regression as a classification method after going through the data augmentation process with an accuracy of 82% and a macro f1-score of 80%, which showed high performance in skin disease detection. Hybrid CNN with machine learning method shows the ability to feature extraction of skin disease images and achieves optimal performance. https://doi.org/10.3390/s22020587 - Wang, Y., Pan, Z., Zheng, J., Qian, L., Li, M.: A hybrid ensemble method for pulsar candidate classification. Abstract Skin diseases have a variety of causes, including exposure to chemicals, sunlight, viruses, bacteria, and other factors. Classification of skin diseases is essential because of their similar symptoms, such as red rashes, itching, and burning. The similar symptoms of the diseases make it difficult to distinguish them visually. The dataset used is MSLD v2.0, which is skin disease image data with 6 classes, namely monkeypox, cowpox, chickenpox, measles, HFMD, and healthy. This research uses three CNN models, namely EfficientNet, DenseNet, and ResNet, as feature extraction. Data augmentation is also applied to increase data variation. What to know There have been outbreaks of clade I monkeypox in Central and Eastern Africa since late 2023. Since January 2024, more than 55,000 confirmed cases of clade I monkeypox have been reported globally, including more than 150 deaths. Newer outbreaks in several Western European countries are likely related to this ongoing outbreak. Transmission dynamics are changing. Only a small proportion of exported clade I monkeypox cases worldwide this year have originated in Central or Eastern African countries. Recent travel-associated clade I monkeypox cases have almost exclusively been attributed to subclade Ib; there have been no deaths associated with these cases and available data have detailed relatively mild disease courses. Outbreak overview In the United States The risk posed by the clade I monkeypox outbreak to most people within the United States remains low. The risk to men who have sex with men is low to moderate. Clade I cases in the United States have increased in frequency since the beginning of March 2026. As of July 2026, there have been more than 30 clade I monkeypox cases reported in the United States. Nearly all U.S. cases were diagnosed in people who: Had recently traveled to areas associated with the outbreak in Central and Eastern Africa; Had recently traveled to parts of Western Europe where newer outbreaks are being reported; OR Were linked to people who had traveled from these areas. CDC expects additional cases in Europe and the United States. Preventing Monkeypox While Traveling Learn where monkeypox is spreading and how to lower your risk of getting it during travel. In Central and Eastern Africa Clade Ia monkeypox outbreaks began impacting western areas of the Democratic Republic of the Congo (DRC) in 2024. Available data indicate that clade Ia monkeypox has spread through sexual contact, regular household contact, and encounters with infected dead or live wild animals. Clade Ib monkeypox cases initially impacted eastern areas of DRC in late 2023. This subclade has driven much of the spread throughout Central and Eastern Africa and most travel-associated cases to other parts of the world. Available data indicate that these cases at first spread through heterosexual intimate or sexual contact between adults, then spread likely occurred within households, including to children. The disease spread in 2024 and 2025 to neighboring countries of DRC, only some of which are endemic for the virus that causes monkeypox, and sustained local spread occurred. As of April 2026, the Democratic Republic of the Congo is still the country with the majority of clade Ib cases. Outside Central and Eastern Africa Several countries in other parts of Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, and South America, as well as Australia, have confirmed clade I monkeypox cases mostly in travelers who'd recently been in areas with clade I outbreaks. To date, there have been more than 300 clade Ib cases in high-income countries, and no deaths have been reported. Beginning in Fall 2025, several countries in Western Europe began reporting clade Ib monkeypox cases among individuals who had no documented history of international travel. These cases were likely related to intimate or sexual exposure among men who have sex with men. We expect additional cases in Europe and the United States. For data since January 1, 2024, see 2022-24 Monkeypox (Monkeypox) Outbreak: Global Trends (shinyapps.io). Confirmed cases include those that are laboratory confirmed as monkeypox virus and may include cases only confirmed as orthopoxvirus. These data are provided for situational awareness and are subject to change. Clade I monkeypox and children Early in the Central and Eastern African outbreak, a high proportion of suspected cases in some areas were reported in children younger than 15 years of age. Historically, cases of monkeypox in children where monkeypox occurs regularly often happen after contact with wild animals that carry the disease. People then can spread the disease to close contacts, including in their households. The number of children with suspected monkeypox in this outbreak is probably due to spread within and between close households, the large number of younger people in affected countries, misdiagnosis of other diseases (such as measles), poor sanitary conditions, limited access to health services, and a high level of food insecurity and malnutrition. Based on what we know today, we don't expect to see the same sort of pattern in the United States for several reasons, including smaller household sizes, access to cleaning and disinfecting products, and improved access to medical care, equipment, and information about preventing spread while caring for patients. Notably, there are no consistent reports of schools as drivers of monkeypox transmission during any recent outbreaks. If cases of clade I monkeypox do happen in children the United States, CDC has clinical and public health guidance for reporting, testing, and effective case management. What CDC is doing CDC has been supporting DRC monkeypox research and response for more than 20 years. CDC and other U.S. government agencies have continued working in-country with partners in affected areas on disease surveillance, building local laboratory capacity, strengthening public health and laboratory workforce capacity, case investigation, case management, infection prevention and control, border health, and risk communication and community engagement. CDC staff brought laboratory supplies and trained local staff on laboratory equipment Resources Monkeypox in the United States and Around the World: Current Situation There are outbreaks of clade I and clade II monkeypox around the world. Outside Central and Eastern Africa Several countries in other parts of Africa, Asia, Europe, North America, and South America, as well as Australia, have confirmed clade I monkeypox cases mostly in travelers who'd recently been in areas with clade I outbreaks. To date, there have been more than 300 clade Ib cases in high-income countries, and no deaths have been reported. Beginning in Fall 2025, several countries in Western Europe began reporting clade Ib monkeypox cases among individuals who had no documented history of international travel. These cases were likely related to intimate or sexual exposure among men who have sex with men. We expect additional cases in Europe and the United States. For data since January 1, 2024, see 2022-24 Monkeypox (Monkeypox) Outbreak: Global Trends (shinyapps.io). Confirmed cases include those that are laboratory confirmed as monkeypox virus and may include cases only confirmed as orthopoxvirus. These data are provided for situational awareness and are subject to change. Clade I monkeypox and children Early in the Central and Eastern African outbreak, a high proportion of suspected cases in some areas were reported in children younger than 15 years of age. Historically, cases of monkeypox in children where monkeypox occurs regularly often happen after contact with wild animals that carry the disease. People then can spread the disease to close contacts, including in their households. The number of children with suspected monkeypox in this outbreak is probably due to spread within and between close households, the large number of younger people in affected countries, misdiagnosis of other diseases (such as measles), poor sanitary conditions, limited access to health services, and a high level of food insecurity and malnutrition. Based on what we know today, we don't expect to see the same sort of pattern in the United States for several reasons, including smaller household sizes, access to cleaning and disinfecting products, and improved access to medical care, equipment, and information about preventing spread while caring for patients. Notably, there are no consistent reports of schools as drivers of monkeypox transmission during any recent outbreaks. If cases of clade I monkeypox do happen in children the United States, CDC has clinical and public health guidance for reporting, testing, and effective case management. What CDC is doing CDC has been supporting DRC monkeypox research and response for more than 20 years. CDC and other U.S. government agencies have continued working in-country with partners in affected areas on disease surveillance, building local laboratory capacity, strengthening public health and laboratory workforce capacity, case investigation, case management, infection prevention and control, border health, and risk communication and community engagement. CDC staff brought laboratory supplies and trained local staff on laboratory equipment Resources Monkeypox in the United States and Around the World: Current Situation There are outbreaks of clade I and clade II monkeypox around the world. Global Health Protection Explore This Topic Search Search Clear Search Public Health What We Do Campaigns and Awareness Days Stories of Impact Resources View all search clear search Global Health Protection Menu clear search Public Health What We Do Campaigns and Awareness Days Stories of Impact Resources View All Home Related Topics Global Health What We Do Campaigns and Awareness Days Stories of Impact Resources View Menu Inside CDC's Guinea Monkeypox Response For Public Health July 31, 2026, visit link for details. At a glance CDC experts worked with Guinea partners to quickly detect, investigate, and respond to a monkeypox outbreak. Prior investments in workforce development and preparedness, including Field Epidemiology Training Program (FETP) training, ensured responders were ready to act when the outbreak emerged. Rapid coordination, strengthened surveillance systems, and community engagement limited transmission and build lasting capacity for future health threats. The Challenge CDC supported the deployment of FETP investigators who conducted contact tracing in affected districts in Conakry and Kindia. In June 2025, Guinea was facing its largest monkeypox outbreak to date. Monkeypox is a viral disease that spreads through close, often intimate contact, causing painful lesions and other symptoms, severe illness, and in some cases, death. What began as a small number of clade II monkeypox cases in Conakry, the nation's capital, soon began to spread. As the outbreak expanded, CDC deployed global health security experts who worked closely with monkeypox subject matter experts and national partners. On-the-ground support helped to rapidly detect, track, and contain the outbreak at its source, moving quickly to contain a potentially deadly virus. Through a coordinated response, CDC played a critical role in slowing transmission, limiting further spread, and reducing the risk of the virus reaching the United States — helping protect communities both abroad and at home. Responding to outbreaks like monkeypox relies on consistent, coordinated efforts from early detection to contact tracing and laboratory confirmation. Together, these steps help reduce spread and protect communities. - Els Mathieu, MD, MPH, CDC Guinea Country Director A Rapidly Expanding Outbreak Early infections were largely among adult men, who often presented with visible monkeypox lesions. Available data suggested the outbreak was spreading through sexual transmission, like patterns seen in neighboring West African countries affected by recent clade I outbreaks. Within weeks, cases spread beyond Conakry into seven regions, with weekly totals surging to as many as 99 nationwide. By December 11, 2025, Guinea had reported 1,894 confirmed cases, including five deaths. The outbreak highlighted the urgent need to find cases faster and strengthen laboratory testing capacity for quicker and more accurate results. It also underscored the importance of tracking individuals who may have been exposed and better understanding how monkeypox was spreading within communities. The situation demanded speed, precision and coordination. Skin lesions on a patient with monkeypox. CDC Support on the Front Lines For more than a decade, CDC had been working with Guinea's Ministry of Health as a trusted partner strengthening disease surveillance, laboratory systems and outbreak response capacity. When the Ministry of Health asked CDC to assist with the outbreak, CDC's experts stepped up. CDC in collaboration with the Ministry of Health, the National Institute of Public Health (INSP), and the National Health Security Agency (ANSS), focused on what mattered most in the moment. Teams worked to find suspected cases sooner, confirm them quicker, and strengthen contact tracing so potential exposures didn't slip through the cracks. They also connected data across teams, turning scattered information into a clearer picture of how the outbreak was unfolding, helping responders move faster. Outbreaks like this don't stop at borders; they require coordination, trust, and real-time action. This response is a reminder that strengthening systems on the ground isn't just about infrastructure — it's about helping countries move faster, act earlier, and ultimately save lives. - CDC Guinea Regional Associate Director Kathleen Gallagher, D.Sc., MPH CDC supported the deployment of eight Field Epidemiology Training Program (FETP) graduates and 18 contact tracers to the most affected districts in Conakry and Kindia over a 12-week period. Both graduates and contact tracers worked case by case — identifying infections, tracing contacts, and helping local health workers respond quickly. Each connection mapped meant another opportunity to stop the virus from spreading further. Strengthening Laboratory Capacity Became Critical CDC Guinea, working with CDC poxvirus laboratory experts, provided technical support to the National Institute of Public Health (INSP). This included helping the laboratory connect to the International Reagent Resource (IRR) platform to directly access the reagents and supplies needed to detect and confirm monkeypox cases. CDC poxvirus laboratory experts also provided virtual training on how to use diagnostic tests capable of identifying viruses like monkeypox, and ensured the laboratories had the tools and supplies needed to carry out testing. Together, this support strengthened INSP's independence, enabling the laboratory to manage its own supply orders and sustain testing capacity without relying on external coordination. Behind the scenes, stronger data systems helped turn information into action. Through support to implementing partner, AFENET, Guinea expanded its use of DHIS2 to track monkeypox cases and strengthen coordination across national response teams, resulting in clearer situational awareness and faster, more targeted decision-making. Closing the Investigation Gap CDC's global health security experts supported a national training that brought together 20 experts from across Guinea to further strengthen the monkeypox response. As the outbreak evolved so did the response. By December, CDC identified a critical gap: the need to better understand how monkeypox was spreading through close and sexual contact, and who was most at risk. Early investigations showed that many cases involved close and sometimes intimate contact, but this information was not being consistently or safely collected. In response, CDC's global health security experts supported a national training that brought together 20 experts from across Guinea to strengthen how sensitive information such as sexual history and close contact exposure was collected during case investigations. The training focused on building skills to ask these questions respectfully, confidentially, and effectively, while collecting information essential for public health action. Those trained are now equipped to extend this knowledge across all 38 of the country's districts, further strengthening outbreak investigations across the nation. Impact That Reaches Beyond Borders Within weeks of the response launch, the trajectory began to shift. Transmission began to slow as districts brought cases under control and chains of infection were interrupted. What had been a rapidly expanding outbreak was contained through coordinated action, local leadership, and sustained technical support. CDC support also extended beyond the immediate response to strengthen core systems needed to sustain and scale Guinea's monkeypox response. This included the work CDC had done improving surveillance and contact tracing, building laboratory testing capacity, and equipping health workers to conduct more effective case investigations. As a result, several districts were able to exit active outbreak status, while stronger data collection enabled more targeted and effective public. Looking Ahead Slowing monkeypox in Guinea not only protected local communities but also helped stop the further spread of the virus and reduce its impact globally, including in the US. Future global health security efforts in the country will focus on expanding training, strengthening integrated surveillance systems, and ensuring Guinea is better prepared to respond quickly to any future outbreaks. Across dozens of countries, CDC is working side by side with partners to detect outbreaks early, respond rapidly, and stop threats before they escalate. In a connected world where disease travels quickly, containing outbreaks at their source reduces the risk of international spread. It's the kind of response and preparedness work that helps protect lives around the world and here at home. Responding to outbreaks like monkeypox relies on consistent, coordinated efforts from early detection to contact tracing and laboratory confirmation. Together, these steps help reduce spread and protect communities. - Els Mathieu, MD, MPH, CDC Guinea Country Director A Rapidly Expanding Outbreak Early infections were largely among adult men, who often presented with visible monkeypox lesions. Available data suggested the outbreak was spreading through sexual transmission, like patterns seen in neighboring West African countries affected by recent clade I outbreaks. Within weeks, cases spread beyond Conakry into seven regions, with weekly totals surging to as many as 99 nationwide. By December 11, 2025, Guinea had reported 1,894 confirmed cases, including five deaths. The outbreak highlighted the urgent need to find cases faster and strengthen laboratory testing capacity for quicker and more accurate results. It also underscored the importance of tracking individuals who may have been exposed and better understanding how monkeypox was spreading within communities. The situation demanded speed, precision and coordination. Skin lesions on a patient with monkeypox. CDC Support on the Front Lines For more than a decade, CDC had been working with Guinea's Ministry of Health as a trusted partner strengthening disease surveillance, laboratory systems and outbreak response capacity. When the Ministry of Health asked CDC to assist with the outbreak, CDC's experts stepped up. CDC in collaboration with the Ministry of Health, the National Institute of Public Health (INSP), and the National Health Security Agency (ANSS), focused on what mattered most in the moment. Teams worked to find suspected cases sooner, confirm them quicker, and strengthen contact tracing so potential exposures didn't slip through the cracks. They also connected data across teams, turning scattered information into a clearer picture of how the outbreak was unfolding, helping responders move faster. Outbreaks like this don't stop at borders; they require coordination, trust, and real-time action. This response is a reminder that strengthening systems on the ground isn't just about infrastructure — it's about helping countries move faster, act earlier, and ultimately save lives. - CDC Guinea Regional Associate Director Kathleen Gallagher, D.Sc., MPH CDC supported the deployment of eight Field Epidemiology Training Program (FETP) graduates and 18 contact tracers to the most affected districts in Conakry and Kindia over a 12-week period. Both graduates and contact tracers worked case by case — identifying infections, tracing contacts, and helping local health workers respond quickly. Each connection mapped meant another opportunity to stop the virus from spreading further. Strengthening Laboratory Capacity Became Critical CDC Guinea, working with CDC poxvirus laboratory experts, provided technical support to the National Institute of Public Health (INSP). This included helping the laboratory connect to the International Reagent Resource (IRR) platform to directly access the reagents and supplies needed to detect and confirm monkeypox cases. CDC poxvirus laboratory experts also provided virtual training on how to use diagnostic tests capable of identifying viruses like monkeypox, and ensured the laboratories had the tools and supplies needed to carry out testing. Together, this support strengthened INSP's independence, enabling the laboratory to manage its own supply orders and sustain testing capacity without relying on external coordination. Behind the scenes, stronger data systems helped turn information into action. Through support to implementing partner, AFENET, Guinea expanded its use of DHIS2 to track monkeypox cases and strengthen coordination across national response teams, resulting in clearer situational awareness and faster, more targeted decision-making. Closing the Investigation Gap CDC's global health security experts supported a national training that brought together 20 experts from across Guinea to further strengthen the monkeypox response. As the outbreak evolved so did the response. By December, CDC identified a critical gap: the need to better understand how monkeypox was spreading through close and sexual contact, and who was most at risk. Early investigations showed that many cases involved close and sometimes intimate contact, but this information was not being consistently or safely collected. In response, CDC's global health security experts supported a national training that brought together 20 experts from across Guinea to strengthen how sensitive information such as sexual history and close contact exposure was collected during case investigations. The training focused on building skills to ask these questions respectfully, confidentially, and effectively, while collecting information essential for public health action. Those trained are now equipped to extend this knowledge across all 38 of the country's districts, further strengthening outbreak investigations across the nation. Impact That Reaches Beyond Borders Within weeks of the response launch, the trajectory began to shift. Transmission began to slow as districts brought cases under control and chains of infection were interrupted. What had been a rapidly expanding outbreak was contained through coordinated action, local leadership, and sustained technical support. CDC support also extended beyond the immediate response to strengthen core systems needed to sustain and scale Guinea's monkeypox response. This included the work CDC had done improving surveillance and contact tracing, building laboratory testing capacity, and equipping health workers to conduct more effective case investigations. As a result, several districts were able to exit active outbreak status, while stronger data collection enabled more targeted and effective public. Looking Ahead Slowing monkeypox in Guinea not only protected local communities but also helped stop the further spread of the virus and reduce its impact globally, including in the US. Future global health security efforts in the country will focus on expanding training, strengthening integrated surveillance systems, and ensuring Guinea is better prepared to respond quickly to any future outbreaks. Across dozens of countries, CDC is working side by side with partners to detect outbreaks early, respond rapidly, and stop threats before they escalate. In a connected world where disease travels quickly, containing outbreaks at their source reduces the risk of international spread. It's the kind of response and preparedness work that helps protect lives around the world and here at home. news.content_title: Atypical Presentation of Mpox as Acute Tonsillitis: A Case Report from the United Arab Emirates
news.content: Mpox can present initially as severe pharyngotonsillitis with significant oropharyngeal luminal narrowing, mimicking acute bacterial infection and preceding the appearance of skin lesions by several days, even in young, immunocompetent patients without recognised epidemiological risk factors. Clinicians should consider Mpox in patients with severe pharyngotonsillitis, particularly when bacterial cultures are negative or when even subtle cutaneous changes appear during admission, to enable timely isolation and appropriate management. A previously healthy 28-year-old man in the United Arab Emirates presented with a two-day history of severe sore throat and painful swallowing that prevented oral intake. Examination revealed bilateral erythematous palatine tonsils with cryptic exudate, an edematous uvula, and pharyngeal erythema. There was no stridor or respiratory distress. Inflammatory markers were elevated (WBC count 14.0 × 109/L; CRP 102 mg/L). Computed tomography of the neck demonstrated bulky, heterogeneous palatine tonsils with significant narrowing of the oropharyngeal lumen and reactive cervical lymphadenopathy; the radiologist’s impression raised the possibility of evolving abscess. A working diagnosis of acute bacterial tonsillitis was made, and intravenous ceftriaxone and dexamethasone were commenced. On hospital day 2, mild non-specific cutaneous lesions appeared, progressing on day 3 to a characteristic vesiculopustular eruption involving the face, trunk, palms, and genital area. Throat culture, finalised on day 4, yielded normal upper respiratory tract flora with no beta-haemolytic streptococci. Real-time PCR on a skin lesion swab confirmed Mpox virus infection (cycle threshold 12). The patient was isolated, transferred to a designated facility on hospital day 9, and discharged home on 11 January 2026 after a total of 27 days from initial admission. A structured post-discharge telephone follow-up on 12 January 2026 confirmed sustained clinical recovery with full lesion resolution and no recurrent symptoms. Mpox typically presents with a prodrome of fever and lymphadenopathy followed by a characteristic vesiculopustular rash. Mpox may present with atypical manifestations, including isolated oropharyngeal, anogenital, and mucosal involvement preceding cutaneous lesions. Recognition of these atypical phenotypes is essential to avoid diagnostic delay and limit secondary transmission, particularly in regions such as the United Arab Emirates and the wider Gulf where published descriptions of atypical presentations remain limited. Introduction Mpox is a zoonotic orthopoxvirus infection that has historically been confined to endemic regions of Central and West Africa. Since May 2022, sustained human-to-human transmission has driven a global outbreak affecting more than 100 countries, prompting the World Health Organization to declare a Public Health Emergency of International Concern in 2022 and again in 2024 following the emergence of clade Ib in central Africa [1,2]. In the United Arab Emirates and the wider Gulf region, sporadic cases have been reported, predominantly linked to international travel [3]; published descriptions of locally relevant atypical clinical presentations remain limited. The classical clinical course consists of a febrile prodrome with lymphadenopathy followed within one to four days by a centrifugal vesiculopustular eruption that progresses through well-defined stages [4]. The 2022 outbreak, however, has been characterized by frequent atypical presentations. Mucosal involvement, including proctitis, urethritis, pharyngitis, and tonsillitis [5, 6], has been described, often preceding or occurring without the classical rash distribution. Severe oropharyngeal lesions causing odynophagia, dysphagia, and significant local inflammation have been documented in case series of clade IIb infection [7]. Such atypical presentations create a real risk of diagnostic delay. Patients may be admitted under alternative working diagnoses, most commonly acute bacterial tonsillitis or peritonsillar infection, and treated with empirical antibacterial therapy and adjunctive corticosteroids before Mpox is considered. This carries implications both for individual patient care and for infection control, as undiagnosed cases may expose healthcare workers and other patients before appropriate isolation is implemented. We report a case of laboratory-confirmed Mpox in a previously healthy, young man in the United Arab Emirates who presented with severe acute tonsillitis and CT evidence of significant oropharyngeal luminal narrowing, in whom the characteristic cutaneous eruption developed only after admission and after initial empirical antibacterial therapy. This case report was prepared in accordance with the CARE (CAse REport) Guidelines [2]. We aim to highlight the clinical features that should prompt consideration of Mpox in patients presenting with severe pharyngotonsillitis, including those without recognized epidemiological risk factors, and to discuss the practical infection-control implications of delayed recognition. To our knowledge, published reports from the United Arab Emirates describing Mpox presenting initially as severe acute tonsillitis with CT-confirmed oropharyngeal narrowing and without clinical airway compromise remain limited. Case Presentation A 28-year-old previously healthy man presented to the emergency department of a regional hospital in the United Arab Emirates with a two-day history of severe sore throat, progressive odynophagia, and inability to tolerate oral intake. He reported no fever, cough, dyspnea, rash, genital symptoms, or gastrointestinal complaints at presentation. He had no chronic medical conditions, took no regular medications, and reported no prior surgeries or known allergies. A detailed epidemiological exposure assessment was performed. The patient denied recent international travel, contact with individuals known to have Mpox or unexplained rash illnesses, healthcare-related exposure, attendance at mass gatherings, overnight stays in shared accommodation or hotels, occupational exposure to potentially infected individuals, recent domestic travel within the United Arab Emirates, and recognized sexual risk factors. Despite comprehensive exposure assessment, no definitive epidemiological source of infection was identified. The patient was alert and hemodynamically stable. Temperature was 37.2°C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 120/91 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. The otolaryngology examination documented bilateral erythematous palatine tonsils with cryptic exudate and no abscess on direct visualization, an erythematous and edematous uvula without deviation, and erythematous pharyngeal mucosa. The oral mucosa was non-erythematous. There was no trismus, no stridor, no respiratory distress, and no drooling. Bilateral tender cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. The skin was documented as moist with no rash at the time of initial examination. Flexible laryngoscopy was not performed. Laboratory studies on admission showed a leucocytosis of 14.0 × 109/L (neutrophils 7.74 × 109/L; lymphocytes 4.63 × 109/L; monocytes 1.25 × 109/L), platelet count 133 × 109/L, and elevated CRP of 102 mg/L. A throat swab obtained at admission in the emergency department was sent for bacterial culture. Given the severity of the progressive odynophagia and inability to tolerate oral intake, CT of the neck was performed to assess for a possible deep neck complication, including an evolving peritonsillar abscess. CT of the neck demonstrated bulky, heterogeneous bilateral palatine tonsils with several ill-defined hypodense areas within and significant narrowing of the oropharyngeal lumen (Figure 1). Multiple enlarged cervical lymph nodes were noted, the largest measuring 14 mm at level III. The nasopharynx, epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, vallecula, pyriform sinuses, vocal cords, laryngeal cartilages, and visualized trachea and esophagus were reported as normal. The radiologist’s impression was “features of tonsillitis with the possibility of evolving abscess.” No follow-up imaging was performed during the admission. Figure 1: CT of the neck on admission An axial non-contrast CT image at the level of the oropharynx demonstrating bulky, heterogeneous bilateral palatine tonsils with ill-defined hypodense areas and significant narrowing of the oropharyngeal lumen. No discrete abscess is identified. Reactive cervical lymphadenopathy was noted on adjacent slices (not shown). The radiologist’s impression was “features of tonsillitis with the possibility of evolving abscess.” The differential diagnosis included acute bacterial tonsillitis, evolving peritonsillar abscess, infectious mononucleosis (Epstein-Barr virus), cytomegalovirus infection, acute HIV seroconversion syndrome, herpes simplex virus infection, Coxsackievirus infection, gonococcal pharyngitis, and other viral causes of severe pharyngotonsillitis. These conditions were considered because of the patient’s prominent oropharyngeal symptoms, elevated inflammatory markers, and the absence of characteristic cutaneous lesions at presentation. The working diagnosis was acute bacterial tonsillitis with possible evolving peritonsillar abscess, and the patient was admitted under joint internal medicine and otolaryngology care. Empirical intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g twice daily and intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg daily were commenced, alongside intravenous fluid support and analgesia. Conservative airway monitoring was implemented; given the absence of stridor or respiratory distress, no airway intervention was indicated. On hospital day 2, the patient developed mild, non-specific cutaneous lesions that did not initially suggest a defined diagnosis. On hospital day 3, the eruption progressed and became clinically characteristic: vesiculopustular lesions appeared on the face, trunk, back, upper limbs, and genital area, evolving sequentially through macular, papular, vesicular, and pustular stages, with several lesions showing central umbilication. Notably, lesions were also present on the palms and dorsa of the hands. The morphology and distribution prompted clinical suspicion of Mpox. The patient was placed in single-room isolation with contact and droplet precautions. A lesion swab was obtained for orthopoxvirus and mpox virus testing. On hospital day 4, the throat swab culture was finalized and reported as the growth of normal upper respiratory tract flora only, with no beta-hemolytic streptococci isolated. On hospital day 6, HIV antigen/antibody combination screening returned negative. Epstein-Barr virus testing showed negative viral capsid antigen IgM, positive viral capsid antigen IgG and nuclear antigen IgG, and undetectable Epstein-Barr virus PCR. Although infectious mononucleosis was considered initially, the emergence of characteristic cutaneous lesions prompted targeted Mpox testing. On hospital day 7, real-time PCR on the skin lesion swab returned positive for the Mpox virus, with a cycle threshold value of 12, consistent with a high viral load. The qualitative assay targeted Mpox virus and other orthopoxviruses using specific primers and probes, with internal and external controls to ensure reliability and detect potential inhibition. Clade-specific identification and additional sexually transmitted infection screening were not performed at our facility. Tecovirimat was not administered because the patient demonstrated progressive clinical improvement with supportive management and local institutional protocols did not recommend antiviral therapy in this setting. Additional sexually transmitted infection screening beyond HIV was not performed because comprehensive sexually transmitted infection testing was not routinely available within our facility at the time of admission and the patient denied recognized sexual risk factors; nevertheless, coinfections with sexually transmitted infections have been reported in Mpox outbreak cohorts and therefore cannot be completely excluded. The patient remained haemodynamically stable throughout admission, with no respiratory deterioration and no requirement for airway intervention. Tonsillar inflammation and oropharyngeal symptoms gradually improved with supportive care, and oral intake was progressively re-established. Cutaneous lesions evolved through pustular and crusting stages without secondary bacterial infection or other complications. Following laboratory confirmation of Mpox on hospital day 7, dedicated written informed consent for clinical photography and publication was obtained from the patient. Representative clinical photographs of the oropharyngeal (Figure 2) and cutaneous (Figure 3) lesions were subsequently obtained on hospital day 9, prior to transfer to the designated isolation facility on the same day. On hospital day 9, in line with national public health protocols, the patient was transferred to a designated Mpox isolation facility for ongoing care. He was discharged home on hospital day 27 in stable clinical condition, with complete resolution of pharyngeal symptoms and progressive healing of cutaneous lesions. Discharge instructions included continued isolation for several days, personal hygiene measures, and clear advice to return if symptoms recurred. A structured post-discharge telephone follow-up was completed on post-discharge day 1; the patient reported feeling well, with all lesions healed, no new lesions, and no recurrent symptoms. The total duration from initial admission to final discharge was 27 days, and no long-term complications were identified. Figure 2: Oropharyngeal lesions Clinical photograph of the oropharynx obtained on hospital day 9, following laboratory confirmation of Mpox and after dedicated written informed consent for clinical photography and publication had been obtained from the patient. The image shows scattered ulcerative and vesiculopustular lesions on the soft palate, tonsillar pillars, and tongue base, accompanied by a small, crusted lesion on the upper cutaneous lip. Figure 3: Cutaneous lesions Representative clinical photographs of cutaneous lesions obtained on hospital day 9, following laboratory confirmation of Mpox and after dedicated written informed consent for clinical photography and publication had been obtained from the patient. The images depict Mpox lesions in pustular and early crusting stages, consistent with the natural evolution of lesions approximately one week after their initial appearance. news.content_original: Mpox can present initially as severe pharyngotonsillitis with significant oropharyngeal luminal narrowing, mimicking acute bacterial infection and preceding the appearance of skin lesions by several days, even in young, immunocompetent patients without recognised epidemiological risk factors. Clinicians should consider Mpox in patients with severe pharyngotonsillitis, particularly when bacterial cultures are negative or when even subtle cutaneous changes appear during admission, to enable timely isolation and appropriate management. A previously healthy 28-year-old man in the United Arab Emirates presented with a two-day history of severe sore throat and painful swallowing that prevented oral intake. Examination revealed bilateral erythematous palatine tonsils with cryptic exudate, an edematous uvula, and pharyngeal erythema. There was no stridor or respiratory distress. Inflammatory markers were elevated (WBC count 14.0 × 109/L; CRP 102 mg/L). Computed tomography of the neck demonstrated bulky, heterogeneous palatine tonsils with significant narrowing of the oropharyngeal lumen and reactive cervical lymphadenopathy; the radiologist’s impression raised the possibility of evolving abscess. A working diagnosis of acute bacterial tonsillitis was made, and intravenous ceftriaxone and dexamethasone were commenced. On hospital day 2, mild non-specific cutaneous lesions appeared, progressing on day 3 to a characteristic vesiculopustular eruption involving the face, trunk, palms, and genital area. Throat culture, finalised on day 4, yielded normal upper respiratory tract flora with no beta-haemolytic streptococci. Real-time PCR on a skin lesion swab confirmed Mpox virus infection (cycle threshold 12). The patient was isolated, transferred to a designated facility on hospital day 9, and discharged home on 11 January 2026 after a total of 27 days from initial admission. A structured post-discharge telephone follow-up on 12 January 2026 confirmed sustained clinical recovery with full lesion resolution and no recurrent symptoms. Mpox typically presents with a prodrome of fever and lymphadenopathy followed by a characteristic vesiculopustular rash. Mpox may present with atypical manifestations, including isolated oropharyngeal, anogenital, and mucosal involvement preceding cutaneous lesions. Recognition of these atypical phenotypes is essential to avoid diagnostic delay and limit secondary transmission, particularly in regions such as the United Arab Emirates and the wider Gulf where published descriptions of atypical presentations remain limited. Introduction Mpox is a zoonotic orthopoxvirus infection that has historically been confined to endemic regions of Central and West Africa. Since May 2022, sustained human-to-human transmission has driven a global outbreak affecting more than 100 countries, prompting the World Health Organization to declare a Public Health Emergency of International Concern in 2022 and again in 2024 following the emergence of clade Ib in central Africa [1,2]. In the United Arab Emirates and the wider Gulf region, sporadic cases have been reported, predominantly linked to international travel [3]; published descriptions of locally relevant atypical clinical presentations remain limited. The classical clinical course consists of a febrile prodrome with lymphadenopathy followed within one to four days by a centrifugal vesiculopustular eruption that progresses through well-defined stages [4]. The 2022 outbreak, however, has been characterized by frequent atypical presentations. Mucosal involvement, including proctitis, urethritis, pharyngitis, and tonsillitis [5, 6], has been described, often preceding or occurring without the classical rash distribution. Severe oropharyngeal lesions causing odynophagia, dysphagia, and significant local inflammation have been documented in case series of clade IIb infection [7]. Such atypical presentations create a real risk of diagnostic delay. Patients may be admitted under alternative working diagnoses, most commonly acute bacterial tonsillitis or peritonsillar infection, and treated with empirical antibacterial therapy and adjunctive corticosteroids before Mpox is considered. This carries implications both for individual patient care and for infection control, as undiagnosed cases may expose healthcare workers and other patients before appropriate isolation is implemented. We report a case of laboratory-confirmed Mpox in a previously healthy, young man in the United Arab Emirates who presented with severe acute tonsillitis and CT evidence of significant oropharyngeal luminal narrowing, in whom the characteristic cutaneous eruption developed only after admission and after initial empirical antibacterial therapy. This case report was prepared in accordance with the CARE (CAse REport) Guidelines [2]. We aim to highlight the clinical features that should prompt consideration of Mpox in patients presenting with severe pharyngotonsillitis, including those without recognized epidemiological risk factors, and to discuss the practical infection-control implications of delayed recognition. To our knowledge, published reports from the United Arab Emirates describing Mpox presenting initially as severe acute tonsillitis with CT-confirmed oropharyngeal narrowing and without clinical airway compromise remain limited. Case Presentation A 28-year-old previously healthy man presented to the emergency department of a regional hospital in the United Arab Emirates with a two-day history of severe sore throat, progressive odynophagia, and inability to tolerate oral intake. He reported no fever, cough, dyspnea, rash, genital symptoms, or gastrointestinal complaints at presentation. He had no chronic medical conditions, took no regular medications, and reported no prior surgeries or known allergies. A detailed epidemiological exposure assessment was performed. The patient denied recent international travel, contact with individuals known to have Mpox or unexplained rash illnesses, healthcare-related exposure, attendance at mass gatherings, overnight stays in shared accommodation or hotels, occupational exposure to potentially infected individuals, recent domestic travel within the United Arab Emirates, and recognized sexual risk factors. Despite comprehensive exposure assessment, no definitive epidemiological source of infection was identified. The patient was alert and hemodynamically stable. Temperature was 37.2°C, heart rate 102 beats per minute, blood pressure 120/91 mmHg, and oxygen saturation 99% on room air. The otolaryngology examination documented bilateral erythematous palatine tonsils with cryptic exudate and no abscess on direct visualization, an erythematous and edematous uvula without deviation, and erythematous pharyngeal mucosa. The oral mucosa was non-erythematous. There was no trismus, no stridor, no respiratory distress, and no drooling. Bilateral tender cervical lymphadenopathy was noted. The skin was documented as moist with no rash at the time of initial examination. Flexible laryngoscopy was not performed. Laboratory studies on admission showed a leucocytosis of 14.0 × 109/L (neutrophils 7.74 × 109/L; lymphocytes 4.63 × 109/L; monocytes 1.25 × 109/L), platelet count 133 × 109/L, and elevated CRP of 102 mg/L. A throat swab obtained at admission in the emergency department was sent for bacterial culture. Given the severity of the progressive odynophagia and inability to tolerate oral intake, CT of the neck was performed to assess for a possible deep neck complication, including an evolving peritonsillar abscess. CT of the neck demonstrated bulky, heterogeneous bilateral palatine tonsils with several ill-defined hypodense areas within and significant narrowing of the oropharyngeal lumen (Figure 1). Multiple enlarged cervical lymph nodes were noted, the largest measuring 14 mm at level III. The nasopharynx, epiglottis, aryepiglottic folds, vallecula, pyriform sinuses, vocal cords, laryngeal cartilages, and visualized trachea and esophagus were reported as normal. The radiologist’s impression was “features of tonsillitis with the possibility of evolving abscess.” No follow-up imaging was performed during the admission. Figure 1: CT of the neck on admission An axial non-contrast CT image at the level of the oropharynx demonstrating bulky, heterogeneous bilateral palatine tonsils with ill-defined hypodense areas and significant narrowing of the oropharyngeal lumen. No discrete abscess is identified. Reactive cervical lymphadenopathy was noted on adjacent slices (not shown). The radiologist’s impression was “features of tonsillitis with the possibility of evolving abscess.” The differential diagnosis included acute bacterial tonsillitis, evolving peritonsillar abscess, infectious mononucleosis (Epstein-Barr virus), cytomegalovirus infection, acute HIV seroconversion syndrome, herpes simplex virus infection, Coxsackievirus infection, gonococcal pharyngitis, and other viral causes of severe pharyngotonsillitis. These conditions were considered because of the patient’s prominent oropharyngeal symptoms, elevated inflammatory markers, and the absence of characteristic cutaneous lesions at presentation. The working diagnosis was acute bacterial tonsillitis with possible evolving peritonsillar abscess, and the patient was admitted under joint internal medicine and otolaryngology care. Empirical intravenous ceftriaxone 1 g twice daily and intravenous dexamethasone 8 mg daily were commenced, alongside intravenous fluid support and analgesia. Conservative airway monitoring was implemented; given the absence of stridor or respiratory distress, no airway intervention was indicated. On hospital day 2, the patient developed mild, non-specific cutaneous lesions that did not initially suggest a defined diagnosis. On hospital day 3, the eruption progressed and became clinically characteristic: vesiculopustular lesions appeared on the face, trunk, back, upper limbs, and genital area, evolving sequentially through macular, papular, vesicular, and pustular stages, with several lesions showing central umbilication. Notably, lesions were also present on the palms and dorsa of the hands. The morphology and distribution prompted clinical suspicion of Mpox. The patient was placed in single-room isolation with contact and droplet precautions. A lesion swab was obtained for orthopoxvirus and mpox virus testing. On hospital day 4, the throat swab culture was finalized and reported as the growth of normal upper respiratory tract flora only, with no beta-hemolytic streptococci isolated. On hospital day 6, HIV antigen/antibody combination screening returned negative. Epstein-Barr virus testing showed negative viral capsid antigen IgM, positive viral capsid antigen IgG and nuclear antigen IgG, and undetectable Epstein-Barr virus PCR. Although infectious mononucleosis was considered initially, the emergence of characteristic cutaneous lesions prompted targeted Mpox testing. On hospital day 7, real-time PCR on the skin lesion swab returned positive for the Mpox virus, with a cycle threshold value of 12, consistent with a high viral load. The qualitative assay targeted Mpox virus and other orthopoxviruses using specific primers and probes, with internal and external controls to ensure reliability and detect potential inhibition. Clade-specific identification and additional sexually transmitted infection screening were not performed at our facility. Tecovirimat was not administered because the patient demonstrated progressive clinical improvement with supportive management and local institutional protocols did not recommend antiviral therapy in this setting. Additional sexually transmitted infection screening beyond HIV was not performed because comprehensive sexually transmitted infection testing was not routinely available within our facility at the time of admission and the patient denied recognized sexual risk factors; nevertheless, coinfections with sexually transmitted infections have been reported in Mpox outbreak cohorts and therefore cannot be completely excluded. The patient remained haemodynamically stable throughout admission, with no respiratory deterioration and no requirement for airway intervention. Tonsillar inflammation and oropharyngeal symptoms gradually improved with supportive care, and oral intake was progressively re-established. Cutaneous lesions evolved through pustular and crusting stages without secondary bacterial infection or other complications. Following laboratory confirmation of Mpox on hospital day 7, dedicated written informed consent for clinical photography and publication was obtained from the patient. Representative clinical photographs of the oropharyngeal (Figure 2) and cutaneous (Figure 3) lesions were subsequently obtained on hospital day 9, prior to transfer to the designated isolation facility on the same day. On hospital day 9, in line with national public health protocols, the patient was transferred to a designated Mpox isolation facility for ongoing care. He was discharged home on hospital day 27 in stable clinical condition, with complete resolution of pharyngeal symptoms and progressive healing of cutaneous lesions. Discharge instructions included continued isolation for several days, personal hygiene measures, and clear advice to return if symptoms recurred. A structured post-discharge telephone follow-up was completed on post-discharge day 1; the patient reported feeling well, with all lesions healed, no new lesions, and no recurrent symptoms. The total duration from initial admission to final discharge was 27 days, and no long-term complications were identified. The image shows scattered ulcerative and vesiculopustular lesions on the soft palate, tonsillar pillars, and tongue base, accompanied by a small, crusted lesion on the upper cutaneous lip. news.content_title: Explosive mpox outbreak causes 3,000 cases in Madagascar
news.content: More than 3,000 cases of mpox have been recorded in Madagascar after the virus spread from a single port city to some of the country's busiest coastal hubs. A total of 3,022 cases and 20 deaths have been recorded as of this week, with cases in Toamasina and Taolagnaro accounting for more than half of all diagnoses. The outbreak has been linked to Clade 1b mpox, a strain that emerged in the Democratic Republic of the Congo in 2024, prompting the World Health Organization (WHO) to declare a global public health emergency at the time. "The main factor driving the continued spread of the disease is human mobility, seeding new outbreaks in areas where the virus has not circulated before," Professor Carlos Maluquer de Motes of the University of Surrey told The Telegraph. "Under-reporting is likely, with the real number of cases exceeding what is being reported." Madagascar is the world's fifth poorest country - Simon Townsley Mpox, formerly known as monkeypox , is a viral disease that causes fever, swollen lymph nodes and a distinctive lumpy rash . It was first identified in monkeys in 1958, with the first human case recorded in 1970 in the Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC). The virus is endemic in parts of Central and West Africa, where it typically spreads from infected animals to humans and then between people through close physical contact. Scientists believe the virus arrived in the Madagascan port city of Mahajanga via sea trading routes early this year, before spreading through the country's commercial transport networks to Toamasina and Taolagnaro. "These are two coastal cities with large commercial activity and consequently movement of people," Prof Maluquer de Motes said. "This facilitated the arrival of the virus and subsequent dissemination across highly dense urban transmission networks." Experts say the true scale of the outbreak may already be larger than official figures suggest. About 65 per cent of mpox tests carried out in Madagascar have come back positive, WHO data shows, which experts believe is a sign that many cases may be going undetected. "The high rate of cases testing positive for mpox indicates surveillance is inadequate," said Dr Jonas Albarnaz, a fellow at the Pirbright Institute. "Limited resources, competing public health priorities, misdiagnosis, and the cultural stigma surrounding mpox can contribute to under-reporting." Young children and those who are pregnant or immunocompromised, including those living with HIV, are at greater risk of developing severe symptoms . Prof Maluquer de Motes said vaccination campaigns should prioritise close contacts of infected people, frontline healthcare workers and other groups at highest risk of exposure. "Populations at the highest risk of infection are sex workers in highly dense urban areas like mining areas or commercial ports, and their contacts," he said. "Of course, frontline healthcare workers will also be at significant risk." Madagascar's Ministry of Health is working with the WHO to expand testing capacity and contact tracing in the worst-affected districts. It remains unclear whether the strain circulating in Madagascar differs in severity from the one that spread in the DRC. In Madagascar, the world's fifth poorest country, vaccine availability and healthcare infrastructure are likely to limit how far immunisation programmes can reach. elements_zh.event: 已确认马达加斯加的 猴痘(进化枝 1b)爆炸物 暴发。该病毒通过人员流动和商业运输网络从马哈赞加传播到图阿马西纳和陶拉尼亚罗。暴发 与 2024 年在刚果民主共和国出现的 Clade 1b 菌株有关,该菌株促使 WHO 发布了全球公共卫生紧急状态声明。
elements_zh.scale_impact_and_risk: 病例:截至本周已记录 3,022 例。死亡人数:20 人记录。传播:人员流动是主要驱动力,在没有事先流通的区域传播新的 暴发。风险:高阳性率(65%)表明漏报;真实病例数可能超过报告数字。严重的症状给弱势群体带来更大的风险。
elements_zh.response_status_and_uncertainty: 回应:马达加斯加卫生部正在与世卫组织合作,扩大受影响最严重地区的检测能力和接触者追踪。正在规划 疫苗接种 活动,优先考虑高风险群体。不确定性:报告不足可能是由于资源有限、卫生优先事项相互竞争、误诊和文化耻辱造成的。目前尚不清楚循环菌株的严重程度是否与刚果民主共和国菌株不同。疫苗 的可用性和医疗基础设施在马达加斯加这个世界第五个最贫穷的国家受到限制。

news.content: ___ Vanguard News Home News Top Stories Politics Metro Business Sports Editorial Columns ALLURE E-editions Search for: Home News Top Stories Politics Metro Business Sports Editorial Columns ALLURE E-editions Home News Politics Metro Business Sports Editorial Columns Allure E-Editions Home » News » Investigation confirms Chickenpox outbreak not Mpox, in Benue community – Health Commissioner News Follow us on Google July 28, 2026 Investigation confirms Chickenpox outbreak not Mpox, in Benue community – Health Commissioner By Peter Duru, Makurdi The Benue State Ministry of Health and Human Services has dismissed reports of a suspected Mpox (Monkeypox) outbreak in Korinya Community, Konshisha Local Government Area, LGA, assuring residents that investigations showed the reported illness was consistent with Chickenpox (Varicella) and not Mpox. The Commissioner for Health and Human Services, Dr. Paul Ogwuche, who disclosed this in a statement he personally signed Monday, said the Ministry swung into action immediately after receiving social media reports on July 25 alleging that residents of Tyokula Achihi Residence, along the Vandeikya-Konshisha Road, had developed fever and widespread blister-like skin rashes suspected to be Mpox. According to him, “The Benue State Ministry of Health and Human Services wishes to reassure the good people of Benue State that the recent social media reports alleging an outbreak of Mpox in Korinya Community have been thoroughly investigated. Based on the findings available at this time, there is no evidence of an Mpox outbreak in Korinya Community, Konshisha LGA.” Dr. Ogwuche explained that the Ministry immediately activated its Public Health Emergency Operations Centre, deploying the Konshisha Local Government Disease Surveillance and Notification Officer, the State Disease Surveillance and Notification Officer, the State Epidemiologist and the World Health Organization (WHO) community surveillance network to verify the claims. He said the investigation identified two adult residents who had earlier developed fever followed by blister-like skin rashes but had already sought treatment at a private health facility and were recovering before the investigation team arrived. The Commissioner stated that a detailed clinical assessment revealed that the illness followed the typical course of Chickenpox, with the patients’ skin lesions already dried and crusted over. He added that there were no lesions on the palms, soles or mouth, which are key clinical features commonly associated with Mpox, while investigators also found no epidemiological link to any confirmed or suspected Mpox case. According to him, “The illness was clinically more consistent with Chickenpox than Mpox. The epidemiological investigation established no known contact with any confirmed or suspected Mpox case, making the likelihood of Mpox considerably lower.” Despite ruling out an Mpox outbreak, Dr. Ogwuche said surveillance had been intensified in Korinya and neighbouring communities, noting that any new suspected cases would have samples collected and sent to the National Reference Laboratory for confirmation in line with Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) protocols. He urged residents to remain calm and avoid spreading unverified information capable of causing unnecessary panic, while commending community members for promptly reporting the suspected illness. The Commissioner reaffirmed the commitment of the administration of Governor Hyacinth Alia to strengthening disease surveillance, emergency preparedness and rapid response systems, assuring that the Ministry would continue to investigate all suspected public health events using globally accepted scientific standards to safeguard the health of Benue residents. news.content: Sunday, August 2, 2026 Follow Us on Google Search Home National Columns Business China News Politics & Power Opinion Entertainment The Sun TV Sporting Sun The Sun Foundation Benue dismisses suspected Mpox in Kornya 28 July 2026 4:12 am WAT By Scholastica Hir Follow Us on Google From Scholastica Hir, Makurdi Benue State Government has dismissed reports of a suspected Mpox outbreak in Korinya Community, Konshisha Local Government Area, saying investigations confirmed the reported cases are clinically consistent with Chickenpox and not Mpox. The Commissioner for Health and Human Services, Dr. Paul Ogwuche, in a statement yesterday in Makurdi, said it launched an immediate investigation after receiving social media reports on July 25, alleging that several residents of Tyokula Achihi along the Vandeikya-Konshisha Road had developed severe fever and blister-like skin rashes suspected to be Mpox. Ogwuche said the report, which generated widespread concern, was treated as a suspected public health event, prompting the activation of the state’s Public Health Emergency Operations Centre (PHEOC), the State Epidemiology Unit and the Disease Surveillance and Notification System. According to him, a joint investigation involving the Konshisha Local Government Disease Surveillance and Notification Officer, the State Disease Surveillance and Notification Officer, the State Epidemiologist and the World Health Organisation (WHO) community surveillance network identified two adult residents who had experienced fever followed by widespread blister-like rashes. He explained that both patients had already sought treatment at a private health facility in Korinya and were showing significant recovery before the investigation team arrived. The ministry said detailed clinical assessment revealed that the illness followed the typical pattern of Chickenpox rather than Mpox. Other News Govt dispels rumours of Mpox outbreak in Benue He noted that the skin lesions had already dried and crusted over, indicating a self-limiting viral infection, while there was no involvement of the palms, soles or oral mucous membranes, features commonly associated with Mpox. He also explained that the investigation also established that neither patient had any known contact with confirmed or suspected Mpox cases, further reducing the likelihood of the disease. He said photographs of the skin lesions and accompanying clinical information reviewed by investigators also supported the conclusion that the illness was clinically compatible with Chickenpox. He said: “Based on the findings available at this time, there is no evidence of an Mpox outbreak in Korinya community in Konshisha LGA.” Despite the findings, the ministry said surveillance had been intensified in Korinya and surrounding communities to ensure that any emerging public health threat is detected promptly. It added that if new suspected cases emerge, clinical samples would be collected and sent to the National Reference Laboratory for laboratory confirmation, in line with Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) surveillance protocols. news.content_original: Sunday, August 2, 2026 Follow Us on Google Search Home National Columns Business China News Politics & Power Opinion Entertainment The Sun TV Sporting Sun The Sun Foundation Benue dismisses suspected Mpox in Kornya 28 July 2026 4:12 am WAT By Scholastica Hir Follow Us on Google From Scholastica Hir, Makurdi Benue State Government has dismissed reports of a suspected Mpox outbreak in Korinya Community, Konshisha Local Government Area, saying investigations confirmed the reported cases are clinically consistent with Chickenpox and not Mpox. The Commissioner for Health and Human Services, Dr. Paul Ogwuche, in a statement yesterday in Makurdi, said it launched an immediate investigation after receiving social media reports on July 25, alleging that several residents of Tyokula Achihi along the Vandeikya-Konshisha Road had developed severe fever and blister-like skin rashes suspected to be Mpox. Ogwuche said the report, which generated widespread concern, was treated as a suspected public health event, prompting the activation of the state’s Public Health Emergency Operations Centre (PHEOC), the State Epidemiology Unit and the Disease Surveillance and Notification System. According to him, a joint investigation involving the Konshisha Local Government Disease Surveillance and Notification Officer, the State Disease Surveillance and Notification Officer, the State Epidemiologist and the World Health Organisation (WHO) community surveillance network identified two adult residents who had experienced fever followed by widespread blister-like rashes. He explained that both patients had already sought treatment at a private health facility in Korinya and were showing significant recovery before the investigation team arrived. The ministry said detailed clinical assessment revealed that the illness followed the typical pattern of Chickenpox rather than Mpox. Other News Govt dispels rumours of Mpox outbreak in Benue He noted that the skin lesions had already dried and crusted over, indicating a self-limiting viral infection, while there was no involvement of the palms, soles or oral mucous membranes, features commonly associated with Mpox. He also explained that the investigation also established that neither patient had any known contact with confirmed or suspected Mpox cases, further reducing the likelihood of the disease. He said photographs of the skin lesions and accompanying clinical information reviewed by investigators also supported the conclusion that the illness was clinically compatible with Chickenpox. He said: “Based on the findings available at this time, there is no evidence of an Mpox outbreak in Korinya community in Konshisha LGA.” Despite the findings, the ministry said surveillance had been intensified in Korinya and surrounding communities to ensure that any emerging public health threat is detected promptly. It added that if new suspected cases emerge, clinical samples would be collected and sent to the National Reference Laboratory for laboratory confirmation, in line with Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC) surveillance protocols. Explore The News magazine → The Benue State Ministry of Health and Human Services has become aware of reports circulating on social media about a suspected Mpox outbreak at the Tyokula Achihi Residence in Korinya, Konshisha Local Government Area. As stated in a statement signed by Dr. Paul Ejeh Ogwuche, Commissioner for Health and Human Services, Benue State, immediately upon the information coming to our attention, the Ministry activated its surveillance system in line with established public health protocols. The Director of Public Health was directed to liaise with the State Epidemiologist, who in turn immediately deployed the Disease Surveillance and Notification Officer (DSNO) for Konshisha Local Government Area to the reported location for on-the-ground assessment, case investigation and collection of appropriate clinical samples for laboratory testing. At this stage, no Mpox outbreak has been confirmed in Benue State. It is important to emphasise that skin rashes and fever can result from several medical conditions, and laboratory confirmation is required before any diagnosis of Mpox can be made. Discover more Health History Skin Conditions The Government of His Excellency, Rev. Fr. Dr. Hyacinth Iormem Alia, places the highest priority on protecting the health of every Benue citizen. Our disease surveillance system remains active across all 23 Local Government Areas, and we maintain close collaboration with the Nigeria Centre for Disease Control and Prevention (NCDC), the Federal Ministry of Health, the World Health Organization (WHO), and other development partners to ensure prompt detection and response to any public health event. The Ministry therefore appeals to members of the public to remain calm and avoid spreading unverified information capable of creating unnecessary panic. We encourage anyone experiencing fever accompanied by unexplained rashes or blisters to report immediately to the nearest health facility for proper medical evaluation and to avoid close physical contact until assessed by healthcare professionals. Discover more Medical Literature & Resources OBGYN Government We commend members of the community for promptly reporting the situation, as early reporting is essential for effective disease surveillance and response. The Ministry will continue to keep the public informed as soon as the investigation and laboratory findings become available. Should the results confirm Mpox or any other disease of public health importance, appropriate response measures will be implemented immediately in accordance with national guidelines. The Benue State Ministry of Health and Human Services remains committed to safeguarding the health and wellbeing of all residents of the state.
